title: Error Spotting
summary: A sentence is split into parts and one part carries a grammatical fault. Errors cluster in a short list — agreement, tense, articles, prepositions, pronouns, correlative pairs and comparison — so a fixed audit order (SVA → tense → article → preposition → pronoun → pairs → word choice) converts this into the most mechanical scoring topic in the section.

subtopics.title: The master checklist: SVA → tense → article → preposition
subtopics.concept:
An error-spotting item gives you four parts of one sentence and asks which part is faulty. Do not hunt vaguely — audit the sentence in a fixed order, because SSC errors follow the same priority ladder in almost every shift.

| Check | Ask yourself | Instant example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Subject–verb | what is the TRUE subject, and how far is it from the verb? | *The quality of the mangoes **were*** → subject = quality (singular) |
| 2. Tense | is there a time anchor? do the clauses agree in time? | ***had** reached* before a later past event |
| 3. Article | sound of the next word? specific or general? | ***an** university* → a university |
| 4. Preposition | which word governs it, and what is its fixed partner? | *insisted **for*** → insisted on |
| 5. Pronoun | case (subject/object)? does it match its antecedent? | *between you and **I*** → me |
| 6. Conjunction/correlative | are both halves of the pair present and parallel? | *No sooner did... **rang*** → ring |
| 7. Comparison / word choice | double comparative? redundancy? wrong confusable? | *more bigger*, *return back* |

**Why an order matters:** about two-thirds of all errors live in checks 1–4. Sweeping in this order catches them before you waste time on stylistic doubts. Also, only ONE part is wrong — the moment one check convicts a part, stop and verify it once, then mark.

**How to verify before marking:** rewrite the sentence correctly in your head. The corrected version must sound like ordinary formal English. If your 'correction' needs restructuring two parts, you have probably misread the sentence; re-run the checklist.

**Where the error usually hides:** the verb part (finite verbs attract agreement and tense errors), the part containing a preposition or article, and the opening part (pronoun case, connectors). Descriptive tail phrases ('of the pending bill') are rarely the answer — they are usually innocent scenery.

**Timing:** 20–25 seconds per question. Read once at normal speed (your ear catches half the errors), then audit with the checklist for the rest.

tricks.title: The 7-step sweep
tricks.body: Verb first: find the subject, check number. Then tense anchors. Then a/an/the by sound. Then preposition partners. Only then pronouns, pairs, and word choice.

example.q: One of my friends / are going / to London / next week.
example.solution: Check 1 (SVA): true subject = 'one' (singular) → 'is going'. Part 2 is the error. Later checks never run.

tricks.title: Strip the middle
tricks.body: Delete phrases between subject and verb ('of my friends', 'of the mangoes', 'as well as the players') and read the bare skeleton — agreement errors become loud.

tricks.title: No-error discipline
tricks.body: When the paper offers 'No error', choose it only after the full sweep; do not pick it because the sentence 'sounds fine' at speed. Roughly one in five such items hides a sneaky SVA or preposition error.

mistakes: Agreeing the verb with the noun nearest to it instead of the true subject.
Marking the part that merely sounds clumsy — awkward is not always wrong.
Overlooking the error in the FIRST part because the eye starts hunting in the middle.
Finding two 'errors' and freezing: re-check the second one; usually it is standard usage you misjudged.

subtopics.title: Subject–verb agreement errors
subtopics.concept:
Agreement errors are the single largest error family in SSC English. The trap is always the same: words are inserted between the true subject and the verb.

| Construction | Rule | SSC-style example |
|---|---|---|
| Each / every / either / neither / everyone / nobody | always singular | *Each of the boys **has** submitted his work.* |
| Either... or / Neither... nor | verb agrees with the NEARER subject | *Neither the manager nor the employees **were** present.* |
| as well as / along with / together with / in addition to | verb follows the FIRST subject | *The captain, as well as the players, **was** fined.* |
| A number of + plural | plural verb | *A number of students **were** absent.* |
| The number of + plural | singular verb | *The number of students **is** small.* |
| One of the + plural noun + who/that | plural verb (relative refers to the plural noun) | *He is one of those officers who **work** late.* |
| One of the + plural noun (no relative) | singular verb for the main clause | *One of my friends **is** going to London.* |
| Uncountables (news, physics, economics) | singular | *The news **is** good.* |
| Plural-form pairs (scissors, trousers) | plural; 'a pair of' → singular | *These trousers **are** new; a pair **is** enough.* |
| Collective nouns | unit → singular; members in disagreement → plural | *The committee **has** decided; the jury **were** divided.* |
| Amounts / distances / periods | single quantity → singular | *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk.* |
| Titles of books / country names | singular even if plural-looking | *'Gulliver's Travels' **is** a satire.* |

**The strip method:** delete every prepositional phrase, 'as well as' cluster, and relative clause between subject and verb, then test number. *The quality of the mangoes **were** not up to the mark* → strip 'of the mangoes' → *the quality ... were* → wrong; *the quality ... was*.

**Relative-clause verbs:** the verb after *who/which/that* agrees with the noun the pronoun points back to. *He is one of those officers who **work** late* (officers work), but *He is the only officer who **works** late* (the only officer).

**Interrupting positives:** *along with, together with, as well as, in addition to, accompanied by, and not* — none of these creates a plural subject. The verb follows the original subject.

**Watch the passive voice too:** agreement errors also appear in passives — *The letters **was** delivered* → *were delivered*.

tricks.title: Subject hunt backwards
tricks.body: From the verb, walk backwards past 'of...' phrases until you hit a noun or pronoun without a preposition in front — that is the subject that decides the verb.

tricks.title: Proximity rule flash
tricks.body: See *neither/nor* or *either/or* with two subjects? The verb matches the second (nearer) subject. Check that, and the item usually collapses instantly.

example.q: Neither the manager nor / the employees was / present at / the meeting.
example.solution: Nearer subject 'employees' is plural → *were present*. Part 2 carries the error.

tricks.title: Quantity is singular
tricks.body: Sums of money, distances, time spans and weights take a singular verb even in plural form: 'Ten kilometres **is** a long walk', 'Five hundred rupees **was** the fine'.

mistakes: Using a plural verb after 'each/every/either' joined to a noun ('Each of the boys have...').
Taking 'a number of' and 'the number of' as the same (plural vs singular).
Making 'news, mathematics, physics' plural because they end in -s.
Agreeing with 'one of the + plural noun' and writing 'who works' — the relative refers to the plural noun.

subtopics.title: Tense and sequence-of-tenses errors
subtopics.concept:
Tense errors come in four reliable shapes.

| Signal | Required tense | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| yesterday, last year, in 1998, ago | simple past | mixing with present perfect |
| already, just, yet, ever, since, for, so far | perfect (present, unless earlier past is meant) | *when I reached, the train **had** already left* |
| since + point of time / for + period | perfect or perfect continuous | *for ten years*, never *since ten years* |
| when-clause / if-clause / as soon as (future meaning) | simple present — no *will* | *I will call you when the meeting **ends**.* |
| earlier of two past actions | past perfect; later action → simple past | *The patient **had died** before the doctor came.* |
| since + past clause | present perfect in main clause | *It **has been** raining since he left.* |
| used to / would | past habit | not *use to* |

**Anchor discipline:** every sentence carries its time information in anchor words. Locate the anchor first; the verb must obey it. *Since ten years* is a double failure — *since* demands a point of time (*since 2015*) and a ten-year span needs *for*.

**Two past events:** the earlier one takes past perfect, the later simple past. But do not demand perfect forms where plain sequence is meant — after *before/after* the perfect is optional if the order is already clear.

**Future-in-clauses:** after *when, before, after, until, as soon as, if* referring to the future, English uses present tense — *I will call you when the meeting **ends*** — never *will end*.

**Reported-speech spillover:** in error-spotting, a reporting verb in the past (*asked, said*) forces backshift in the reported clause: *He asked why he **had** failed*, not *why did he fail* (word order also reverts to statement order).

**Perfect-continuous partners:** *has/have been + -ing* pairs with *since/for*: *She has been working here **for** ten years*.

tricks.title: Underline every anchor
tricks.body: Circle yesterday/ago/since/for/by the time/when/next week before judging any verb. Most tense questions answer themselves once the anchors are visible.

example.q: When I reached / the station, the train / already left / without a whistle.
example.solution: Two past events: reaching came after the train's leaving → earlier event needs past perfect: *had already left*. Part 3.

tricks.title: Will-check
tricks.body: Scan for *will* inside a *when/if/until* clause with future meaning — SSC plants this trap repeatedly.

tricks.title: Since/for sorting
tricks.body: *Since* + starting point (since Monday, since 2019, since childhood); *for* + duration (for ten years, for a week). Wrong partner = wrong part.

mistakes: Using present perfect with a finished-time anchor ('I have met him yesterday').
Backshifting only half a sentence: 'He said he **will** come' → 'would come'.
Choosing past perfect wherever two past verbs appear, even in simple chronological narration.
Writing 'since + duration' because it sounds formal.

subtopics.title: Article and preposition errors
subtopics.concept:
**Articles.** Three decisions cover everything:
- *a/an* — chosen by the FIRST SOUND of the next word, not its letter: *a university, a European, a one-rupee coin* (yu/w sounds); *an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an x-ray* (vowel sounds, silent h).
- *the* — for a specific/known noun, a unique thing (*the sun*), a superlative (*the best*), an ordinal (*the first*), and a noun restricted by the phrase after it (*the girl in blue*).
- zero article — before most proper nouns, meals, languages, abstract nouns in general use, and school/college/hospital in their purpose sense (*go to school*).

**Prepositions.** SSC tests fixed partners, not spatial logic. When you see a preposition, find its governor (the verb, adjective or noun it hangs on) and recall the pair.

| Governor | Partner | Governor | Partner |
|---|---|---|---|
| insist | on | arrive | at (a point) / in (a city) |
| depend | on | angry | with (person) / at (thing) |
| apologise | to (person) for (act) | good | at (skill) / for (health) |
| married | to | different | from |
| prefer | to | senior / junior / superior / inferior | to (never than) |
| afraid / fond / aware / proud | of | reason / cause | for / of |
| solution / answer / key | to | influence / effect / impact | on |
| consist | of | deal / cope | with |
| congratulate | on | suffer | from |
| compare | to (liken) / with (contrast) | comply | with |

**Common placements:** *arrive AT a station, IN a city*; *consists OF*; *die OF a disease, FROM a wound*; *deprived OF*; *capable OF*; *different FROM*; *prefer X TO Y*; *abide BY*; *accordING TO* (never *according with*).

**Double-check the whole part:** prepositions often sit quietly at the end of a long part ('...in a garden near an university') — read prepositions individually instead of skimming the part as a whole.

tricks.title: Say it aloud
tricks.body: Articles are sound decisions. Pronounce the phrase — 'an university' fails the ear immediately ('yu' sound), 'a honest man' likewise.

example.q: The children / were playing / in a garden / near an university.
example.solution: 'University' begins with the *yu* consonant sound → *a university*. Part 4.

tricks.title: Governor chant
tricks.body: Underline the word the preposition depends on and recite its partner: insist—on, angry—with (person), prefer—to, married—to. Wrong partner = the answer.

tricks.title: The-with-superlative scan
tricks.body: Superlative adjectives and ordinals demand *the*: 'the most intelligent girl', 'the first attempt'. A bare superlative is a hidden article error.

mistakes: Choosing *an* before words starting with a vowel LETTER that sounds like a consonant (university, union, one).
Using *than* after senior/junior/superior/inferior/prefer instead of *to*.
Saying 'angry on him' or 'consists in students' from literal translation.
Inserting *the* before 'school/hospital/home' in the purpose sense ('go to the school' when meaning 'attend').

subtopics.title: Pronoun and correlative-conjunction errors
subtopics.concept:
**Pronoun case.** Subject forms (I, he, she, we, they, who) do the action; object forms (me, him, her, us, them, whom) receive it or follow a preposition:
- after prepositions: *between you and **me***, *for him and **me***;
- after *let*: *Let him and me try*;
- comparing with a hidden verb: *She is taller than **I** (am)*.

**Pronoun–antecedent agreement:** *each, everyone, somebody, nobody, either* take singular pronouns (*Each of the boys... his assignment*). Collective nouns take *it* (as units) or *they* (as members).

**Unnecessary pronouns:** *My friend he came... / The book, it is...* — a pronoun duplicating the subject is an error.

**Correlative pairs.** The classic SSC items:

| Pair | Correct shape | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| No sooner... than | *No sooner did the bell **ring** than...* | using *when*, or past tense after *did* |
| Hardly / Scarcely... when | *Hardly had he **sat** down when...* | using *than* |
| Not only... but also | parallel structures after both halves | joining noun with clause |
| Either... or / Neither... nor | verb agrees with nearer subject | verb agreeing with first subject |
| Both... and | *Both Ram **and** his brother...* | *both... as well as* |
| Lest... should | *Work hard lest you **should** fail.* | *lest... will not* |
| Such... as / such... that | *Such books as... / such a noise that...* | mixing the two |
| Whether... or | *I asked whether he **would** come or not.* | *whether... nor* |

**Parallelism under pairs:** whatever follows *not only* must match in form what follows *but also* (noun with noun, clause with clause). *She not only sings but also dances* — parallel verbs. Mixing forms is itself the planted error.

**No sooner forms:** with *did* → base verb (*No sooner did the bell **ring** than...*); with *had* → past participle (*No sooner had the bell **rung** than...*). Both shapes are standard; mixing shapes is not.

tricks.title: Preposition + I? Kill it
tricks.body: Any 'between you and I', 'for he and I' construction is wrong in standard English — object form after a preposition, every time.

example.q: Between you and I, / the new manager / has no / practical experience.
example.solution: Preposition takes object form → *between you and me*. Part 1.

tricks.title: Did + base form
tricks.body: After *did/does/do*, the verb loses its tense: *No sooner did the bell ring*. A past form after *did* is a guaranteed error.

tricks.title: Partner visibility test
tricks.body: Cover the sentence except the pair words. If one half of a correlative appears without its partner, or with the wrong partner (*hardly... than*), that part is the error.

mistakes: Using *whom* as a subject or *who* after a preposition ('to who').
Writing 'one of my friend' (plural noun needed) or 'between him and she'.
Pairing *hardly/scarcely* with *than* and *no sooner* with *when* — the two pairs are swapped.
Making 'everyone... their' the error without noticing the paper accepts singular *their* in informal use — SSC's answer key follows *his/her*; mark accordingly when options force a choice.

subtopics.title: Comparison, redundancy and confusable-word errors
subtopics.concept:
**Comparison rules.**
- Double comparative/superlative is always wrong: *more bigger, most fastest*.
- Compare like with like: *The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi* (climate vs climate, not climate vs city).
- *than any other + singular* when the subject belongs to the group: *Mumbai is bigger than **any other** city in India* — without *other*, Mumbai is compared with itself.
- Latin comparatives take *to*, never *than*: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer* → *to*.
- *elder* takes no *than* and applies within families; *older than* everywhere else.

**Redundancy.** English rejects pairs that repeat one idea: *return back, repeat again, revert back, final conclusion, close proximity, sufficient enough, cooperate together, mutual friendship between the two*. Strike the second word.

**Confusables:**

| Pair | Distinction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| few / a few | *few* = almost none (negative); *a few* = some (positive) | *Few men are wise; a few students stayed back.* |
| little / a little | *little* = hardly any; *a little* = some | *There is a little water left.* |
| much / many | *much* + uncountable; *many* + countable | *much help, many friends* |
| fewer / less | *fewer* + countable; *less* + uncountable | *fewer books, less sugar* |
| elder / older | *elder* only for family, no *than*; *older* with *than* | *my elder brother; older than I* |
| farther / further | *farther* = distance; *further* = additional | *further details* |
| lie / lay | *lie* (recline) — lay, lain; *lay* (put) — laid | *He lay down; he laid the pen down.* |
| return back / repeat again / revert back | redundant pairs — drop the second word | *He returned at midnight.* |

**Word-order errors** also land here: in embedded questions the statement order returns — *He asked why he **had failed***, not *why did he fail*. And adverbs of frequency precede the main verb but follow *be*: *He always is* → *He is always*.

tricks.title: -er/-more clash scan
tricks.body: Look for *more* glued to a comparative (*more bigger*) or *most* glued to a superlative — instant error, no further thought needed.

example.q: Delhi is / more bigger / than Agra / in area.
example.solution: *bigger* is already comparative; *more* doubles it → Part 2. Correct: *Delhi is bigger than Agra*.

tricks.title: Back-and-forth redundancy hunt
tricks.body: Two-word pairs where the second word repeats the first are planted answers: return BACK, repeat AGAIN, revert BACK. Train the eye to flinch at them.

tricks.title: that-of insertion test
tricks.body: In comparisons of two nouns' qualities, the second noun needs *that of/those of*: 'The roads of Delhi are wider than **those of** Patna'. Missing *those of* = comparison error.

mistakes: Writing 'Mumbai is bigger than any city in India' and missing the missing *other*.
Using *than* after prefer/senior/junior because 'than' compares — these five take *to* only.
Treating 'a little/a few' as errors — they are positive forms; *little/few* alone are the negative ones.
Flagging standard phrases as redundant because they are long ('in spite of the fact that' is wordy but not the marked error in SSC items).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A verb separated from its subject by 'of...', 'as well as...', or a relative clause; each/either/neither constructions; a number of vs the number of.
pyqPatterns.approach: Strip the interrupting phrases, find the true subject, apply number — proximity rule for or/nor pairs.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Anchors like yesterday, since, for + period, already, when-clause with future meaning, or two past events in one sentence.
pyqPatterns.approach: Underline anchors, then fit each verb to its anchor; earlier-of-two past events takes past perfect; no 'will' in time clauses.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: a/an before vowel-letter-but-consonant-sound words (university, one, European) or the reverse (hour, honest, MBA); missing 'the' before superlatives/unique nouns.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pronounce the phrase; apply the sound rule, then check specificity for 'the'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A fixed-partner verb/adjective/noun followed by a preposition that feels off: insisted for, angry on, good in (skill), consists from.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the governor, recall the standard pair, and compare letter by letter.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Pronoun after a preposition in subject form; duplicated subject pronoun; one half of no sooner/hardly/not only with a wrong or absent partner.
pyqPatterns.approach: Apply case rules for pronouns; verify both halves of any correlative and the verb form after did/had.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: more + -er, most + -est, missing other in any-other comparisons, than after Latin comparatives, pairs like return back.
pyqPatterns.approach: Scan for doubled comparison markers, then check that both sides of the comparison are the same kind of thing.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The quality of the mangoes / imported from Maharashtra / were not / up to the mark.
solvedExamples.solution: The true subject is *quality* (singular); 'of the mangoes' is an interrupting phrase and 'imported from Maharashtra' a reduced relative clause — neither changes the number. Singular subject → *was not up to the mark*. Checklist position: check 1 (SVA) convicts part 3 before any later check runs.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Strip the middle: 'the quality ___' → was. Agreement first, always.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

I will call you / when the meeting / will end / this evening.
solvedExamples.solution: In a time clause (*when, before, until, as soon as, if*) pointing to the future, English uses the simple present: *when the meeting **ends***. The *will* belongs only in the main clause ('I will call you'). Checklist position: check 2 (tense anchors) — the anchor is the future main clause.
solvedExamples.shortcut: No *will* after when/if/until. Present tense carries the future meaning in the clause.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

No sooner did / the bell rang / than the students / rushed out of the class.
solvedExamples.solution: *No sooner* pairs with *than* (part 3 is correct), and after auxiliary *did* the main verb must be the base form: *No sooner did the bell **ring***. Part 2's past form *rang* duplicates the tense that *did* already supplies. Checklist position: check 6 (correlative pairs and verb shape).
solvedExamples.shortcut: See 'did' → expect the base verb. 'No sooner... rang' is a planted duplicate-tense error.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

One of my friends / are going / to London / next week.
practice.solution: The subject is *one*, not *friends*: 'one of my friends **is** going'. The phrase 'of my friends' merely modifies *one*.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Neither the manager nor / the employees was / present at / the monthly meeting.
practice.solution: With *neither... nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — *employees* (plural) → **were** present. *Was* wrongly agrees with the distant singular subject.
practice.shortcut: Or/nor pair → match the second subject.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Each of the boys / have submitted / his assignment / well before the deadline.
practice.solution: *Each* is invariably singular: 'Each of the boys **has** submitted'. Note that part 3 (*his*) is correct — a singular pronoun after *each* is exactly what standard grammar wants.
practice.shortcut: 'Each of ___' → singular verb, even though the nearest noun is plural.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The captain, as well as / the players, were / congratulated by / the cricket board.
practice.solution: *As well as* does not build a plural subject; the verb follows the first subject, *the captain* → **was** congratulated. If the sentence meant both equally, it would use *and*.
practice.shortcut: 'As well as' is a intruder, not a conjunction of number — verb follows subject one.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

When I reached / the platform, the train / already left / under a thick cover of fog.
options: under a thick cover of fog.
practice.solution: Two past events in sequence: the train's leaving happened before the reaching → earlier event takes past perfect: *the train **had already left***. Signal words: *when I reached* + *already*.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

She has been / working in this college / since ten years / and enjoys every day of it.
options: and enjoys every day of it.
practice.solution: *Since* takes a point of time (*since 2015*); a duration takes **for**: *for ten years*. The perfect continuous 'has been working' is itself correct with either partner — the partner is what failed.
practice.shortcut: Since = starting point, for = length. 'Since ten years' breaks the pair.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The children / were playing / in a garden / near an university.
practice.solution: *University* begins with the consonant sound *yu*, so it takes **a**: 'near a university'. The article follows sound, not spelling.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Sita is / the most intelligent / girl in / a class.
practice.solution: A noun made specific by the superlative phrase and the limiting phrase 'in...' takes **the**: *the most intelligent girl in the class*. 'A class' leaves the noun unidentified and unidiomatic.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The professor / was visibly angry / on the students / for their repeated excuses.
practice.solution: *Angry* takes **with** a person and **at** a thing: 'angry with the students'. *On* is not a partner of *angry* in standard usage.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

He insisted / for immediate payment / of the two months' / pending electricity bill.
practice.solution: *Insist* pairs with **on**: 'insisted on immediate payment'. Part 3's possessive (*two months'*) is correct as a time-denoting possessive.
practice.shortcut: Insist—on. Recall the pair, not the meaning.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Between you and I, / the newly appointed / manager has no / practical field experience.
practice.solution: A preposition takes object forms: *between you and **me***. *I* is a subject form and cannot follow *between*.
practice.shortcut: Preposition + I is always the error; flip it mentally: 'between me'.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Hardly had / the chief guest arrived / than the power / went off.
practice.solution: *Hardly/Scarcely* pair with **when**; *no sooner* pairs with *than*. The sentence mixes the two pairs: 'Hardly had... **when** the power went off'.
practice.shortcut: Two fixed pairs: hardly...when, no sooner...than. Swapped partners = the answer.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Mumbai is / more bigger / than any other city / in the state.
practice.solution: *Bigger* is already comparative; adding *more* creates a double comparative: *Mumbai is bigger than any other city in the state*. Part 3 is correct — *any other* is exactly what the comparison needs, since Mumbai itself belongs to the group of cities.
practice.shortcut: Double comparative = instant conviction: -er and 'more' cannot coexist.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The exhausted traveller / returned back / to the hotel / a little after midnight.
practice.solution: *Return* already contains the idea of coming back; *back* is redundant: *returned to the hotel*. Redundant pairs are planted answers — return back, repeat again, revert back.
practice.shortcut: Hear the pair: return + back repeats one idea. Strike the second word.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The interviewer asked / my friend that why / he had left / his previous job.
practice.solution: After *asked*, the reported clause drops **that** when the question word *why* introduces it: 'asked my friend why he had left'. *That* and *why* cannot introduce the same clause. (The backshift to *had left* in part 3 is correct.)
practice.shortcut: In indirect questions, the wh-word alone introduces the clause — 'asked that why' doubles the introducer.
